newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police denounced after 100 protesters hurt.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police denounced after 100 protesters hurt.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's security police attacked thousands of peaceful pro-democracy demonstrators overnight, injuring more than 100 in the bloodiest political violence seen for years in Belgrade.

A co-leader of the opposition coalition urged followers to arm themselves for another demonstration on Monday, a call that could signal an ominous turn to almost three months of peaceful pro-democracy rallies.

Another leader of the Zajedno (Together) party bloc, which has been protesting at election fraud by the authoritarian leftist government, said the sudden police crackdown might mean emergency rule was just around the corner.

Vesna Pesic, a veteran human rights campaigner in her 50s who was clubbed in the back and thigh by police, said emergency measures could pre-empt any legal ruling reinstating Zajedno's victory in municipal elections.
It would also override the expiry on Tuesday of the current Socialist-led city council's mandate, Pesic told reporters.
"This regime no longer has any option but to beat people."
State television (RTS), Milosevic's main media mouthpiece, said police struck on Sunday night only to clear crowds who were blockading the Brankov Bridge, one of Belgrade's major traffic arteries.

The demonstrators were actually only trying to file across the bridge to a central square for their usual evening rally, an angle not reported by RTS. Traffic would have been jammed for a maximum half an hour if they had been allowed to proceed, as they had on several previous nights.
Six weeks ago the interior ministry banned marches that blocked traffic but has only sporadically enforced the measure.

Opposition activists vowed they would not be intimidated by the police assault, believed ordered by neo-communist hardliners in the security apparatus, and summoned supporters to another rally at 3 p.m. (1400 gmt) on Monday.

"All of Belgrade must go into the streets on Monday ... Our protest will be peaceful, but all participants must take with them something they can use to defend themselves," said Vuk Draskovic, co-leader of Zajedno.
"There can be no more Gandhi-style resistance to this madness," he told independent student Radio Index.

Police in helmets and body armour turned central Belgrade into a battleground, repeatedly charging marchers demanding the restoration of opposition victories in elections in 14 large Serbian municipalities, including the capital Belgrade.

Most of the 20,000 marchers gathering for the 77th straight day of protests quickly dispersed in the face of truncheon charges backed up by water cannon, some of whose blasts were apparently laced with a tear-gas chemical.
But some stood their ground in the subzero mid-winter cold, retaliating by hurling stones, bricks and bottles.
Some protesters tried to parry police by lighting piles of car tyres and tossing concrete slabs into the streets.
Local journalists said the aggressive action by uniformed security police had been unseen in Belgrade since 1991 when Milosevic called in tanks to quell pro-democracy rallies.

Presiding doctors at two major Belgrade emergency clinics said about 130 people were admitted for treatment of injuries ranging from limb fractures to broken teeth. Ambulances also tended to countless minor casualties in the midst of melees.
Police also pummelled several television cameramen including Reuters' Sergei Karazy, smashed their equipment and seized videotapes in at least one case.

France and Germany condemned the police action as Western support for democracy campaigners in Serbia grew. The French government, in a significant policy switch, invited the three Zajedno leaders to visit Paris as soon as possible.

"This invitation amounts to recognition by the French government of the leaders of the Zajedno opposition coalition, which through the past weeks has proved its political maturity," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said.
"(France) solemnly warns the Serbian authorities against a slide into violence which can only lead to a disastrous outcome for their country," he said.
De Charette demanded that Milosevic abide by the conclusions of an OSCE mission which investigated the elections in Serbia and verified that the opposition had won them.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Milosevic's intolerance of opposition was jeopardising any chance for closer Yugoslav links to the European Union.
But he also urged Serbia's opposition not to be provoked into abandoning its strict adherence to non-violence.
Until now, Socialist authorities had seemed indecisive in the face of unrelenting protests, hesitating to use violence that might provoke renewed international isolation of Serbia.

Senior churchmen and soldiers have joined the opposition in demanding recognition of the November 17 local election gains, while teachers are on strike, schools are shut, universities in turmoil and lawyers rallying on the streets.
